entry.title: Are You a Boiling Frog? 🐸
entry.summary: Imagine this: A frog is placed in a pot of water. If the water is boiling, the frog will immediately jump out. But if the water is cold and slowly heated, the frog fails to notice the gradual rise in temperature and eventually boils to death. We often think disasters strike suddenly. But life’s real danger is incremental decay. It’s not the massive failure that kills you—it’s the quiet, almost invisible erosion of your potential, your energy, and your clarity. The twist most people miss: the frog isn’t just being boiled by external circumstances—it’s being boiled by its own tolerance. You normalize discomfort. You justify mediocrity. You let stress and inertia grow slowly until they define your reality. Deliberate Discomfort Example: take a cold shower, speak up in a tense meeting, or learn something extremely hard. Purpose: retrain your tolerance, so slow harm feels intolerable. Temperature Checks, Not Audits Reverse-Boil Thinking Use Friction as Feedback If something feels uncomfortable or draining, treat it as a warning signal, not an annoyance. The frog ignores the heat. You shouldn’t.

In this post, I explore the differences between Ruby and Elixir in the context of asynchronous programming. To do so, I first developed a simple crawler application in both languages and then compared their approaches to handling concurrency. Elixir Task module: urls |> Enum.map(fn url -> Task.async(fn -> Wanderer.crawl(url) end) end) |> Enum.map(fn t -> Task.await(t, 30_000) end)
